Four studies looked at ways to improve adherence to HIV medication in children. No single way was studied twice. Two studies were done in low-income countries. Two studies were randomized controlled trials, and two were not.

A home-based nursing program was studied in one trial and was found to improve knowledge and medication refills, but not CD4 count or viral load. A second trial looked at caregiver medication diaries and found no significant difference in missed doses or CD4 percentage or viral load.

A non-randomized trial of peer support group therapy for adolescents found no change in self-reported adherence, but the percentage of participants with suppressed viral load increased. A second non-randomized trial found no difference in adherence between children on different types of medication, but more children on one type had suppressed viral load.

A home-based nursing intervention may help improve adherence to HIV medication, but more evidence is needed. Medication diaries do not seem to affect adherence or disease outcomes. Two interventions, an LPV/r-containing regimen and peer support therapy for adolescents, did not show improvements in adherence, but they did show greater viral load suppression compared to control groups. More well-designed studies of interventions to improve pediatric adherence to HIV medication are needed.
